{{Short description|Operator in quantum mechanics}}
In [[quantum mechanics]], the '''position operator''' is the [[operator (physics)|operator]] that corresponds to the position [[observable]] of a [[Subatomic particle|particle]].

When the position operator is considered with a wide enough domain (e.g. the space of [[tempered distributions]]), its [[eigenvalue]]s are the possible [[position vector]]s of the particle.<ref>{{cite book |title=Quanta: A handbook of concepts | first1=P.W. |last1=Atkins|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=1974|isbn=0-19-855493-1}}</ref>

In one dimension, if by the symbol <math display="block"> | x \rangle</math> we denote the [[Unitary operator|unitary]] eigenvector of the position operator corresponding to the eigenvalue <math>x</math>, then, <math> |x \rangle </math> represents the state of the particle in which we know with certainty to find the particle itself at position <math>x</math>.

Therefore, denoting the position operator by the symbol <math>X</math> we can write <math display="block"> X| x\rangle = x |x\rangle,</math> for every real position <math>x</math>.

One possible realization of the unitary state with position <math>x</math> is the [[Dirac delta function|Dirac delta]] (function) distribution centered at the position <math>x</math>, often denoted by <math>\delta_x</math>.

In quantum mechanics, the ordered (continuous) family of all Dirac distributions, i.e. the family
<math display="block">\delta = (\delta_x)_{x \in \R},</math>
is called the (unitary) position basis, just because it is a (unitary) eigenbasis of the position operator <math>X</math> in the space of [[tempered distributions]].

It is fundamental to observe that there exists only one linear continuous operator <math>X</math> on the space of tempered distributions to itself, such that
<math display="block">X(\delta_x) = x \delta_x,</math>
for every real point <math>x</math>. It is possible to prove that the unique operator <math>X</math> is necessarily defined by
<math display="block">X(\psi) = \mathrm x \psi,</math>
for every tempered distribution <math>\psi</math>, where <math>\mathrm x</math> denotes the coordinate function of the position line{{snd}} defined as the inclusion of the real line into the complex plane i.e
<math display="block">\mathrm x : \Reals \to \Complex : x \mapsto x .</math>

==Introduction==

Consider representing the [[quantum state]] of a particle at a certain instant of time by a [[square integrable]] [[wave function]] <math> \psi </math>. For now, assume one space dimension (i.e. the particle "confined to" a straight line). If the wave function is [[Probability amplitude#Normalization|normalized]], then the [[square modulus]]
<math display="block"> |\psi|^2 = \psi^* \psi ,</math>
represents the [[probability amplitude|probability density]] of finding the particle at some position <math> x </math> of the real-line, at a certain time. That is, if
<math display="block"> \|\psi\|^2 = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} |\psi|^2 d \mathrm x = 1,</math>
then the probability to find the particle in the position range <math>[a,b]</math> is
<math display="block"> \pi_X (\psi)([a,b]) =\int_a^b |\psi|^2 d \mathrm x .</math>

Hence the [[expected value]] of a measurement of the position <math> X </math> for the particle is
<math display="block">\langle X \rangle_{\psi} = \int_\R \mathrm x |\psi|^2 d \mathrm x = \int_\R \psi^* (\mathrm x \psi) \, d \mathrm x= \langle \psi | X(\psi) \rangle,</math>
where <math> \mathrm x </math> is the coordinate function
<math display="block"> \mathrm x : \Reals \to \Complex : x \mapsto x ,</math>
which is simply the [[embedding|canonical embedding]] of the position-line into the complex plane.

Strictly speaking, the observable position <math> X =\hat{\mathrm x}</math> can be point-wisely defined as
<math display="block">\left(\hat{\mathrm x} \psi\right) (x) = x\psi(x) ,</math>
for every wave function <math>\psi </math> and for every point <math> x </math> of the real line. In the case of equivalence classes <math>\psi \in L^2</math> the definition reads directly as follows
<math display="block">\hat{\mathrm x} \psi = \mathrm x \psi , \quad \forall \psi \in L^2.</math>
That is, the position operator <math> X </math> multiplies any wave-function <math> \psi </math> by the coordinate function <math> \mathrm x </math>.

===Three dimensions===

The generalisation to three dimensions is straightforward.

The space-time wavefunction is now <math> \psi(\mathbf{r}, t) </math> and the expectation value of the position operator <math> \hat \mathbf{r} </math> at the state <math> \psi </math> is
<math display="block"> \left\langle \hat \mathbf{r} \right\rangle _\psi = \int \mathbf{r} |\psi|^2 d^3 \mathbf{r} </math>
where the integral is taken over all space. The position operator is
<math display="block">\mathbf{\hat{r}}\psi = \mathbf{r}\psi.</math>

==Basic properties ==

In the above definition, which regards the case of a particle confined upon a line,  the careful reader may remark that there does not exist any clear specification of the [[Domain of a function|domain]] and the [[co-domain]] for the position operator. In literature, more or less explicitly, we find essentially three main directions to address this issue.

# The position operator is defined on the subspace <math> D_X </math> of <math> L^2 </math> formed by those equivalence classes <math> \psi </math> whose product by the embedding <math> \mathrm x </math> lives in the space <math> L^2 </math>. In this case the position operator <math display="block"> X : D_X \subset L^2 \to L^2 : \psi \mapsto \mathrm x \psi </math> reveals not continuous (unbounded with respect to the topology induced by the canonical scalar product of <math> L^2 </math>), with no eigenvectors, no eigenvalues and consequently with empty [[point spectrum]].
# The position operator is defined on the [[Schwartz space]] <math> \mathcal S </math> (i.e. the [[nuclear space]] of all smooth complex functions defined upon the real-line whose derivatives are rapidly decreasing). In this case the position operator <math display="block"> X : \mathcal S \subset L^2  \to \mathcal S \subset L^2  : \psi \mapsto \mathrm x \psi </math> reveals ''continuous'' (with respect to the canonical topology of <math> \mathcal S </math>), injective, with no eigenvectors, no eigenvalues and consequently with empty point spectrum. It is (fully) [[Self-adjoint operator|self-adjoint]] with respect to the scalar product of <math> L^2 </math> in the sense that <math display="block"> \langle X (\psi)|\phi\rangle = \langle \psi|X(\phi)\rangle, \quad \forall \psi,\phi \in \mathcal S.</math> 
# The position operator is defined on the [[dual space]] <math> \mathcal S^\times </math> of <math> \mathcal S </math> (i.e. the nuclear space of [[Spaces of test functions and distributions|tempered distributions]]). As <math>L^2</math> is a subspace of <math> \mathcal S^\times</math>, the product of a tempered distribution by the embedding <math> \mathrm x </math> always lives <math> \mathcal S^\times </math>. In this case the position operator <math display="block"> X : \mathcal S^\times \to \mathcal S^\times : \psi \mapsto \mathrm x \psi </math> reveals ''continuous'' (with respect to the canonical topology of <math> \mathcal S^\times </math>), surjective, endowed with complete families of generalized  eigenvectors and real generalized eigenvalues. It is self-adjoint with respect to the scalar product of <math> L^2 </math> in the sense that its [[Transpose of a linear map|transpose operator]] <math display="block"> {}^tX : \mathcal S \to \mathcal S : \phi \mapsto \mathrm x \phi , </math> is self-adjoint, that is <math display="block"> \left\langle\left. \,{}^tX (\phi)\right|\psi \right\rangle = \left\langle \phi| \,{}^tX(\psi)\right\rangle, \quad \forall \psi,\phi \in \mathcal S. </math>

The last case is, in practice, the most widely adopted choice in Quantum Mechanics literature, although never explicitly underlined.{{citation needed|date=October 2024}} It addresses the [[Spectral theorem#Possible absence of eigenvectors|possible absence of eigenvectors]] by extending the Hilbert space to a [[rigged Hilbert space]]:{{sfn|de la Madrid Modino|2001|loc=chpt. 2.6}} 
<math display="block">\mathcal S \subset L^2 \subset \mathcal S^\times,</math>
thereby providing a mathematically rigorous notion of eigenvectors and eigenvalues.{{sfn|de la Madrid Modino|2001|pp=104-117}}

==Eigenstates==

The [[eigenfunction]]s of the position operator (on the space of tempered distributions), represented in [[Position and momentum space#Position and momentum spaces in quantum mechanics|position space]], are [[Dirac delta functions]].

'''''Informal proof.''''' To show that possible eigenvectors of the position operator should necessarily be Dirac delta distributions, suppose that <math> \psi </math> is an eigenstate of the position operator with eigenvalue <math> x_0 </math>. We write the eigenvalue equation in position coordinates,
<math display="block"> \hat{\mathrm x}\psi(x) = \mathrm x \psi(x) = x_0 \psi(x) </math>
recalling that <math> \hat{\mathrm x} </math> simply multiplies the wave-functions by the function <math> \mathrm x </math>, in the position representation. Since the function <math> \mathrm x </math> is variable while <math> x_0 </math> is a constant, <math> \psi </math> must be zero everywhere except at the point <math> x_0 </math>. Clearly, no [[continuous function]] satisfies such properties, and we cannot simply define the wave-function to be a complex number at that point because its <math>L^2</math>-norm would be 0 and not 1. This suggest the need of a "functional object" ''concentrated'' at the point <math> x_0 </math> and with integral different from 0: any multiple of the Dirac delta centered at <math> x_0 </math>.
The normalized solution to the equation
<math display="block"> \mathrm x \psi = x_0 \psi </math>
is
<math display="block"> \psi(x) = \delta(x - x_0),</math> or better <math display="block">\psi = \delta _{x_0},</math>
such that
<math display="block"> \mathrm x \delta_{x_0} = x_0 \delta_{x_0} .</math>
Indeed, recalling that the product of any function by the Dirac distribution centered at a point is the value of the function at that point times the Dirac distribution itself, we obtain immediately
<math display="block"> \mathrm x \delta_{x_0} = \mathrm x (x_0) \delta_{x_0} =x_0 \delta_{x_0} .</math>
Although such Dirac states are physically unrealizable and, strictly speaking, are not functions, the Dirac distribution centered at <math> x_0 </math> can be thought of as an "ideal state" whose position is known exactly (any measurement of the position always returns the eigenvalue <math> x_0 </math>). Hence, by the [[uncertainty principle]], nothing is known about the momentum of such a state.

==Momentum space==

Usually, in quantum mechanics, by representation in the momentum space we intend the representation of states and observables with respect to the canonical unitary momentum basis
<math display="block">
\eta = \left(\left[
(2\pi\hbar)^{-\frac{1}{2}} e^{(\iota/\hbar) (\mathrm x|p)}\right]\right)
_{p \in \R}.
</math>

In [[momentum space]], the position operator in one dimension is represented by the following differential operator
<math display="block"> \left(\hat{\mathrm x}\right)_P = i\hbar\frac{d}{d \mathrm p} = i\frac{d}{d \mathrm k}, </math>

where:
* the representation of the position operator in the momentum basis is naturally defined by <math> \left(\hat{\mathrm x}\right)_P (\psi)_P = \left(\hat{\mathrm x}\psi\right)_P </math>, for every wave function (tempered distribution) <math>\psi</math>;
* <math>\mathrm p</math> represents the coordinate function on the momentum line and the wave-vector function <math>\mathrm k</math> is defined by <math>\mathrm k = \mathrm p / \hbar </math>.

==Formalism in ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''', '''C''')==

Consider the case of a [[Spin (physics)|spin]]less particle moving in one spatial dimension. The [[state space (physics)|state space]] for such a particle contains <math> L^2(\Reals,\Complex) </math>; the Hilbert space of [[complex number|complex-valued]], [[square-integrable function]]s on the [[real line]].

The position operator is defined as the [[self-adjoint operator]]
<math display="block">Q : D_Q \to L^2(\Reals, \Complex) : \psi \mapsto \mathrm q \psi,</math>
with [[domain of definition]]
<math display="block">D_Q = \left\{ \psi \in L^2(\R) \mid \mathrm q \psi \in L^2(\R) \right\},</math>
and coordinate function <math> \mathrm q : \Reals \to \Complex </math> sending each point <math> x \in \R </math> to itself, 
such that<ref>{{cite book |title=Quantum Mechanics Demystified|url=https://archive.org/details/isbn_9780071471411 |url-access=registration|first1=D. |last1=McMahon|edition=2nd|publisher=Mc Graw Hill|year=2006|isbn=0-07-145546-9}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Quantum Mechanics|first1=Y. |last1=Peleg|first2=R.|last2= Pnini|first3=E.|last3= Zaarur|first4=E.|last4= Hecht|edition=2nd|publisher=McGraw Hill|year=2010|isbn=978-0071623582}}</ref>
<math display="block">Q (\psi)(x) = x \psi (x) = \mathrm q(x) \psi (x),</math>
for each pointwisely defined <math> \psi \in D_Q </math> and <math> x \in \R </math>.

Immediately from the definition we can deduce that the [[Spectrum (functional analysis)|spectrum]] consists of the entire real line and that <math>Q</math> has a strictly [[Decomposition of spectrum (functional analysis)#Decomposition into absolutely continuous, singular continuous, and pure point|continuous spectrum]], i.e., no discrete set of eigenvalues.

The three-dimensional case is defined analogously. We shall keep the one-dimensional assumption in the following discussion.

==Measurement theory in ''L''<sup>2</sup>('''R''', '''C''')==

As with any quantum mechanical [[observable]], in order to discuss position [[measurement]], we need to calculate the spectral resolution of the position operator
<math display="block">X : D_X \to L^2(\Reals, \Complex) : \psi \mapsto \mathrm x \psi </math>
which is
<math display="block">X = \int_\R \lambda \, d \mu_X(\lambda) = \int_\R \mathrm x \, \mu_X = \mu_X (\mathrm x),</math>
where <math>\mu_X</math> is the so-called [[Projection-valued measure|spectral measure]] of the position operator.

Let <math>\chi _B</math> denote the [[indicator function]] for a [[Borel subset]] <math>B</math> of  <math>\mathbb{R}</math>. Then the spectral measure is given by 
<math display="block"> \psi \mapsto \mu_X(B)(\psi) = \chi_B \psi ,</math> i.e., as multiplication by the indicator function of <math>B</math>.

Therefore, if the [[system (physics)|system]] is prepared in a state <math>\psi</math>, then the [[probability]] of the measured position of the particle belonging to a [[Borel set]] <math>B</math> is
<math display="block"> \|\mu_X(B)(\psi)\|^2 = \|\chi_B \psi\|^2 = \int_B |\psi|^2\ \mu =\pi_X(\psi)(B),</math>
where <math>\mu</math> is the Lebesgue measure on the real line.

After any measurement aiming to detect the particle within the subset B, the wave function [[wave function collapse|collapses]] to either
<math display="block"> \frac{\mu_X(B) \psi}{\|\mu_X(B) \psi \|} = \frac{\chi_B \psi}{\| \chi_B \psi \|}</math>
or
<math display="block"> \frac{(1 - \chi_B)\psi}{\|(1 - \chi_B)\psi\|},</math>
where <math>\| \cdot \|</math> is the Hilbert space norm on <math>L^2(\Reals, \Complex)</math>.
